title: Eaters of Bacteria
topic: bacteriophage therapy, its eclipse and its return
paragraphs: In 1915, the English bacteriologist Frederick Twort noticed something odd on his culture plates.
Some bacterial colonies had turned glassy, as if dissolving, and material from a dissolved colony passed the effect to a fresh one.
Twort reported this in The Lancet, suggested a virus might be responsible, and then, short of money and distracted by war, set the question aside.
Two years later, at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, Felix d'Herelle described an invisible agent that destroyed the bacteria of dysentery and named it: bacteriophage, the eater of bacteria.
A long quarrel over credit followed, but the discovery itself was secure.
A bacteriophage, or phage for short, is a virus that infects only bacteria.
They are thought to be the most abundant biological entities on Earth.
The classic phage looks like a tiny lunar lander: a protein head holding its genes, a tail, and gripping fibers.
Infection follows a sequence that microbiologists call the lytic cycle.
The phage attaches to a specific receptor molecule on the bacterial surface, injects its genome into the cell, and redirects the cell's own machinery to copy that genome and build new phage parts.
Within as little as half an hour, new viruses fill the cell, and phage enzymes break open the cell wall from the inside.
The cell bursts, releasing tens to hundreds of phages, each ready to begin again; a dense culture can clear within hours.
Not every phage kills on arrival.
Some, called temperate phages, can instead insert their genome into the bacterial chromosome and lie quiet, copied with the host at each division, a state called lysogeny.
Such a dormant phage, a prophage, may wake after many generations, often when its host is damaged, and turn lytic.
Lysogeny has a darker side for medicine.
A prophage can carry genes that change its host's behavior, and the toxins behind cholera and diphtheria are encoded on genes acquired this way.
A temperate phage can also shuttle antibiotic resistance genes from one bacterium to another.
So a phage chosen for therapy should be strictly lytic: it must kill reliably, and it must not be able to settle in and hand its host new tricks.
Phages are also choosy, and their choosiness cuts both ways.
Because a phage must recognize a particular receptor, it usually infects only certain strains within a single species, sometimes only a handful.
For the patient, this is a gift: a phage aimed at a wound infection will leave the trillions of helpful bacteria in the gut untouched, while a broad-spectrum antibiotic scorches friend and foe alike.
For the physician, it is a burden.
The infecting strain must be isolated, grown, and tested against a library of phages, which can take days a very sick patient may not have.
An antibiotic can be pulled from a shelf; a phage, in most cases, must be matched.
The decades after d'Herelle's report were giddy ones.

He was treating patients by 1919, companies in Europe and the United States sold phage preparations for everything from dysentery to boils, and Sinclair Lewis built his 1925 novel Arrowsmith around a young doctor testing phages against plague.
The evidence, however, did not keep pace.
Many early trials had no control groups, some commercial products were found to contain little or no active phage, and the lysogeny problem was not yet understood.
In 1934, a long review in the Journal of the American Medical Association found most claims unsupported, and the field's reputation in the West never recovered.
Then came penicillin.
By the late 1940s, antibiotics were cheap, stable, broad, and backed by controlled trials, and most Western physicians saw no reason to look back.
The story did not end everywhere.

In 1923, the Georgian microbiologist George Eliava, who had worked with d'Herelle in Paris, founded an institute in Tbilisi that became a center of phage work, and d'Herelle himself came to work there in the 1930s.
Eliava was executed in Stalin's purges in 1937, but the institute that now bears his name survived, and phage therapy became routine in Soviet medicine.
Short of antibiotics, Soviet physicians prescribed phages for wound and intestinal infections for decades, and the institute built one of the world's largest phage collections.
Most of it appeared in Russian journals Western scientists did not read, and much of it lacked the controlled design that Western medicine had come to demand, so it was easy to ignore.
There was a scientific reason for caution too, the same one now troubling antibiotics: evolution.
Bacteria exposed to a phage soon produce mutants that the phage cannot infect, most often by altering or shedding the surface receptor the phage uses to attach.
Bacteria also carry internal defenses that chop up foreign DNA; CRISPR, now a gene-editing tool, began as a bacterial memory of past phage attacks.
Phage therapists answer with cocktails: mixtures of several phages that attack the same bacterium through different receptors, so that a mutant which escapes one phage is still caught by another.
There is a further, more hopeful twist.

Resisting a phage often costs the bacterium something: the discarded receptor may have been needed to cause disease or to pump out antibiotics, so a resistant mutant can end up newly vulnerable to drugs that had failed.
That twist played out in the case that revived Western interest.

In late 2015, Tom Patterson, a professor at the University of California, San Diego, fell ill in Egypt with an infection of Acinetobacter baumannii, a bacterium notorious for resisting nearly every antibiotic.
By early 2016 he was in a coma and out of antibiotics, and his wife, the epidemiologist Steffanie Strathdee, began calling laboratories about phage therapy.
Within weeks, researchers at Texas A&M University and at a United States Navy laboratory had each screened their collections against his isolate and assembled cocktails that killed it.
With emergency permission from the Food and Drug Administration, his physicians infused phages into his abscess and then into his bloodstream in March 2016.
Patterson woke within days, and over the following months, with phages and antibiotics given together, the infection cleared.
Tellingly, the bacterium did evolve resistance to the phages, but the resistant form appeared more sensitive to an antibiotic in his regimen.

The case was published in 2017, and the effect was immediate: UC San Diego opened a phage therapy center in 2018, requests poured into phage laboratories worldwide, and compassionate-use treatments have since been reported for lung infections, infected implants, and other infections antibiotics could no longer touch.
Yet an honest reader should notice what these reports are: single cases, tried because nothing else remained, and often published because they succeeded.
The patients who did not improve rarely make the news, and a therapy cannot be judged on its best days.
The deepest obstacle may be regulatory, and it follows from the biology.
Drug approval normally rests on a fixed, well-characterized product made the same way every time.

A phage cocktail is none of those things: it is alive, it reproduces inside the patient, it may need reformulating as the bacterium changes, and the ideal mixture for one patient is wrong for the next.

United States regulators have so far granted case-by-case emergency permission rather than approving any phage as a medicine, while Belgium lets pharmacists prepare phages for individual patients under a defined quality standard.
The first phage products accepted by American regulators were not drugs at all but food sprays, the earliest approved in 2006 against Listeria on ready-to-eat meats.
Whether phage therapy becomes ordinary medicine depends on work far less dramatic than a bedside rescue.
It will require randomized trials, of which few have been run, with mixed results; phage banks that match an isolate in hours, not days; and manufacturing standards for a product that evolves.
The need is not in doubt: antibiotic-resistant infections now cause more than a million deaths a year worldwide, and few new antibiotics are coming.
A century after Twort watched his colonies dissolve, the eaters of bacteria are back on the table.
They are not a miracle, and anyone who promises one has not read the history, but for the first time since the 1930s they have a fair chance to prove what they can do.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the agent d'Herelle described in 1917 destroyed the bacteria responsible for
choices: dysentery
cholera
plague
boils
diphtheria

proof.quote: destroyed the bacteria of dysentery

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says d'Herelle described an invisible agent that destroyed the bacteria of dysentery. The other diseases do appear in the passage, but each is attached to a different idea.
distractorNotes: Cholera appears in paragraph 3 as a toxin carried on phage genes, not as d'Herelle's target.
Plague is the disease in Sinclair Lewis's novel in paragraph 5.
Boils are among the conditions commercial phage products were sold for in paragraph 5.
Diphtheria is paired with cholera in paragraph 3 as a phage-encoded toxin.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 1, the word 'secure' most nearly means
choices: kept under guard
safe from theft
tightly fastened
emotionally confident
beyond dispute

proof.quote: but the discovery itself was secure

questions.why: Paragraph 1 sets the quarrel over credit against the discovery itself, which was 'secure': the finding stood firm no matter who got the credit. The everyday sense of safety or locks does not fit a discovery.
distractorNotes: Being guarded is the physical sense again; nothing in the sentence is being protected.
Safety from theft is the everyday sense of 'secure' and cannot describe a scientific finding.
Fastening is the physical sense of the word, which does not apply to a discovery.
Confidence describes a person, and the sentence is about the discovery, not the people.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT described in paragraph 2 as part of the lytic cycle?
choices: The phage injects its genome into the cell.
The phage genome is inserted into the bacterial chromosome.
Phage enzymes break open the cell wall from the inside.
The cell's own machinery is redirected to build new phage parts.
The phage attaches to a receptor on the bacterial surface.

proof.quote: attaches to a specific receptor molecule on the bacterial surface
injects its genome into the cell
redirects the cell's own machinery to copy that genome and build new phage parts
phage enzymes break open the cell wall from the inside
insert their genome into the bacterial chromosome

questions.why: Paragraph 2 lists attachment, injection, hijacking of the cell's machinery, and bursting out. Inserting the genome into the chromosome is lysogeny, which paragraph 3 presents as the alternative to the lytic cycle.
distractorNotes: Injection of the genome is stated in the same sentence of paragraph 2.
Enzymes breaking the wall open from the inside is in paragraph 2, sentence 6.
Redirecting the cell's own machinery is stated in paragraph 2, sentence 5.
Attachment is the first step named in paragraph 2, sentence 5.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a temperate phage would be a poor choice for therapy even if it could kill the target bacterium because it
choices: cannot recognize receptors on most bacterial strains
reproduces too slowly to clear a dense infection
might give the bacterium harmful new genes
has never been tested in a controlled clinical trial
would be destroyed by the bacterium's CRISPR defenses

proof.quote: A prophage can carry genes that change its host's behavior
it must not be able to settle in and hand its host new tricks

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says a prophage can carry toxin genes and shuttle antibiotic resistance between bacteria, then concludes that a therapeutic phage must not 'settle in and hand its host new tricks.' The danger is gene transfer, not killing power.
distractorNotes: Receptor specificity belongs to paragraph 4 and applies to all phages, not temperate ones in particular.
Speed of reproduction is never raised as a weakness of temperate phages.
Trial history is discussed in paragraphs 5 and 11 and is never tied to temperate phages.
CRISPR appears in paragraph 7 as a general bacterial defense, not a special weakness of temperate phages.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a phage's narrow host range benefits the patient because the phage
choices: can be pulled from a shelf like an antibiotic
spares the helpful bacteria in the gut
cannot be resisted by the infecting bacterium
kills a wider range of strains than an antibiotic does
can be matched to the infecting strain within hours

proof.quote: will leave the trillions of helpful bacteria in the gut untouched

questions.why: Paragraph 4 calls specificity a gift for the patient because a targeted phage leaves the helpful gut bacteria untouched, while a broad-spectrum antibiotic 'scorches friend and foe alike.'
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says the opposite: an antibiotic comes off a shelf, while a phage must be matched.
Paragraph 7 says bacteria do evolve resistance to phages.
Reversed: the phage's range is narrower than an antibiotic's, not wider.
Matching takes days in paragraph 4; hours is the goal paragraph 11 hopes for.

questions.stem: The author mentions Sinclair Lewis's novel Arrowsmith in paragraph 5 primarily to
choices: explain why the 1934 review was so harshly critical
suggest that phage therapy was effective against plague
give an example of a controlled trial of phage therapy
show that novelists understood phage biology better than physicians did
illustrate how far early excitement about phages had spread

proof.quote: The decades after d'Herelle's report were giddy ones.
Sinclair Lewis built his 1925 novel Arrowsmith around a young doctor testing phages against plague

questions.why: Paragraph 5 opens by calling the decades after d'Herelle 'giddy ones' and then stacks up examples: d'Herelle's patients, commercial products, and a popular novel. The novel is there to show that the excitement reached beyond the laboratory into popular culture.
distractorNotes: The review is introduced three sentences later and is explained by the weak evidence, not by the novel.
The author never claims phages worked against plague; the novel is fiction.
A novel is not a trial, and the passage says early trials lacked control groups.
The passage makes no comparison between novelists and physicians.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following contributed to the decline of phage therapy in the West EXCEPT
choices: the arrival of cheap, stable antibiotics
a critical review published in 1934
trials that lacked control groups
evidence that phages carried toxin genes
commercial products that contained little or no active phage

proof.quote: Many early trials had no control groups
some commercial products were found to contain little or no active phage
In 1934, a long review
antibiotics were cheap, stable
the lysogeny problem was not yet understood

questions.why: Paragraph 5 names uncontrolled trials, inactive products, the 1934 review, and the arrival of antibiotics. It says the lysogeny problem was 'not yet understood' at the time, so toxin genes could not have driven the decline.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 ends with penicillin and the cheap, stable antibiotics of the late 1940s.
The 1934 review is in paragraph 5, sentence 5.
Stated in paragraph 5, sentence 4.
Stated in the same sentence of paragraph 5.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the institute in Tbilisi
choices: was founded by d'Herelle himself in the 1930s
was the first to test phage therapy in controlled clinical trials
closed after its founder was executed in 1937
was founded by a scientist who had worked with d'Herelle
published most of its findings in Western journals

proof.quote: George Eliava, who had worked with d'Herelle in Paris, founded an institute in Tbilisi

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says George Eliava, who had worked with d'Herelle in Paris, founded the Tbilisi institute in 1923. d'Herelle only visited, in the 1930s.
distractorNotes: d'Herelle visited in the 1930s, but Eliava founded it in 1923.
Paragraph 6 says much of the Soviet work lacked controlled design.
Paragraph 6 says the institute survived Eliava's execution.
Paragraph 6 says most of the work was published in Russian, in journals Western scientists did not read.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Western scientists ignored the Soviet phage work mainly because
choices: it was out of their sight and lacked rigorous design
the Eliava Institute refused to share its phage collection
it had been shown to be fraudulent after Eliava's death
the 1934 review had already proven that phages could not work
Soviet physicians used phages only for intestinal infections

proof.quote: much of it lacked the controlled design that Western medicine had come to demand, so it was easy to ignore

questions.why: Paragraph 6 closes by saying the work was in Russian, in journals Western scientists did not read, and lacked controlled design, 'so it was easy to ignore.' Language and method, not disproof, kept it out of view.
distractorNotes: The passage says the institute built a large collection, not that it refused to share it.
Nothing in the passage calls the Soviet work fraudulent.
The 1934 review found Western claims unsupported, which is not the same as proving phages cannot work.
Paragraph 6 names wound infections as well as intestinal ones.

questions.stem: According to the passage, bacteria most often become resistant to a phage by
choices: producing enzymes that destroy the phage's protein head
altering or losing the receptor the phage attaches to
using CRISPR to chop up the phage's DNA
pumping the phage out of the cell before it can replicate
acquiring resistance genes from a prophage

proof.quote: most often by altering or shedding the surface receptor the phage uses to attach

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says resistant mutants arise 'most often by altering or shedding the surface receptor the phage uses to attach.' DNA-chopping defenses and CRISPR are mentioned next as additional defenses, not the most common route.
distractorNotes: The passage never mentions enzymes attacking the phage head.
CRISPR is named in paragraph 7 as a further defense, not the most common one.
Pumps appear in paragraph 7 as a way bacteria expel antibiotics, not phages.
Prophages shuttle antibiotic resistance genes in paragraph 3, not resistance to phages.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle behind the phage cocktails described in paragraph 7?
choices: A farmer rotates crops from year to year so that a pest adapted to one crop starves the next year
A hospital switches to a different antibiotic each month so that no single drug is overused
A laboratory screens fifty candidate phages against a patient's bacterial strain to find the single one that kills it fastest
A patient takes three drugs that hit a virus at different steps, so a mutant escaping one is stopped by the others
A doctor doubles the dose of an antibiotic when the first course fails to clear an infection

proof.quote: so that a mutant which escapes one phage is still caught by another

questions.why: Paragraph 7 describes cocktails as several attackers used at once, through different routes, so that an escape from one is caught by another. Three antiviral drugs given together at different steps follow the same logic. Rotation and bigger doses are different strategies.
distractorNotes: Crop rotation changes the target over time; a cocktail attacks the same target several ways at once.
Rotating one drug at a time is sequential, not several attackers at once.
Screening for the single best phage is the matching problem of paragraph 4, not a cocktail.
A higher dose of the same agent gives a mutant nothing new to escape from.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the phages used to treat Tom Patterson were supplied by
choices: his wife's own laboratory at UC San Diego
a university in Texas and a Navy laboratory
a company that sold phage products in the 1930s
the Food and Drug Administration's phage bank
the Eliava Institute in Tbilisi and a Belgian pharmacy

proof.quote: researchers at Texas A&M University and at a United States Navy laboratory

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says researchers at Texas A&M University and at a United States Navy laboratory each screened their collections against Patterson's isolate and assembled cocktails that killed it.
distractorNotes: Strathdee is an epidemiologist who called laboratories; the passage never gives her a phage lab.
Commercial products of the 1930s belong to paragraph 5, not to the 2016 case.
The FDA gave emergency permission; the passage never says it holds phages.
The Eliava Institute and Belgium appear in other paragraphs and had no part in this case.

questions.stem: The passage implies that Patterson's recovery, by itself, cannot settle whether phage therapy works because
choices: the Food and Drug Administration refused to approve the treatment
the bacterium never developed resistance to the cocktail
he also received antibiotics and his case was one patient
the phages were given only into the abscess and never reached his blood
his case was published without peer review

proof.quote: with phages and antibiotics given together
single cases, tried because nothing else remained, and often published because they succeeded

questions.why: Paragraph 8 notes the phages and antibiotics were given together, and paragraph 9 warns that such reports are single cases, often published because they succeeded. One patient on two treatments cannot show which one worked.
distractorNotes: The FDA granted emergency permission; it did not refuse.
Paragraph 8 says the bacterium did evolve resistance.
Paragraph 8 says the phages went into his abscess and then into his bloodstream.
The passage says the case was published in 2017 and says nothing about review.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the future of phage therapy is best described as
choices: cautiously optimistic
uncritically enthusiastic
nostalgic and regretful
openly dismissive
coldly indifferent

proof.quote: They are not a miracle, and anyone who promises one has not read the history, but for the first time since the 1930s they have a fair chance to prove what they can do.
a therapy cannot be judged on its best days

questions.why: The last paragraph says phages are 'not a miracle' and warns against anyone who promises one, yet gives them 'a fair chance to prove what they can do.' Paragraph 9 adds that a therapy cannot be judged on its best days. Hope with the brakes on is cautious optimism.
distractorNotes: The author explicitly warns against promises of a miracle and against judging on best days.
The author looks forward to trials, not backward with regret.
A dismissive author would not say the need is not in doubt or give phages a fair chance.
Indifference does not fit an author who calls the need beyond doubt.

questions.stem: The author mentions food sprays in paragraph 10 primarily to
choices: praise the Food and Drug Administration for its early approval in 2006
argue that phages are safer in food than in patients
highlight how little ground phages have gained as approved medicines
show that Listeria is the bacterium phages kill best
explain why Belgium adopted a different regulatory approach from the United States

proof.quote: rather than approving any phage as a medicine
were not drugs at all but food sprays

questions.why: Paragraph 10 is about the regulatory obstacle. Right after saying no phage has been approved as a medicine in the United States, the author notes that the first accepted phage products were food sprays, 'not drugs at all,' which underlines how far phages still are from approval as medicine.
distractorNotes: The sentence is pointed, not congratulatory; it stresses what has not happened.
The passage never compares safety in food with safety in patients.
Listeria is simply the target of the spray; no claim about 'best' is made.
Belgium's approach is stated in the previous sentence and is not explained by the food sprays.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Belgium differs from the United States in that Belgium
choices: lets pharmacists prepare phages for single patients
grants emergency permission on a case-by-case basis
requires a randomized trial before any phage may be used
has approved a phage cocktail as a licensed medicine
restricts phages to use on ready-to-eat foods

proof.quote: Belgium lets pharmacists prepare phages for individual patients under a defined quality standard

questions.why: Paragraph 10 contrasts the United States, which grants case-by-case emergency permission, with Belgium, which lets pharmacists prepare phages for individual patients under a defined quality standard.
distractorNotes: Case-by-case emergency permission is the United States approach in the same sentence.
The passage calls for randomized trials in paragraph 11 but attributes no such requirement to Belgium.
Neither country is said to have approved a phage as a licensed medicine.
Food sprays are the United States example in the next sentence.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Regulators should refuse to approve any medicine that is alive and changes inside the patient.
Bacteriophages are the most abundant organisms on Earth and will soon replace antibiotics.
Tom Patterson's recovery proved that phage cocktails can cure any antibiotic-resistant infection.
Phage therapy was abandoned in the West because the Soviet Union controlled the only phage collections.
Phage therapy, eclipsed by antibiotics, is returning with real promise and unresolved problems.

proof.quote: bacteriophage, the eater of bacteria
most Western physicians saw no reason to look back
the case that revived Western interest
they have a fair chance to prove what they can do

questions.why: The passage walks from the discovery (paragraph 1) through the eclipse by antibiotics (paragraph 5), the revival after Patterson's case (paragraph 8), and the trials and regulatory problems still ahead (paragraphs 10 and 11). The answer captures the whole arc without overreaching.
distractorNotes: The passage describes the regulatory problem but never argues that regulators should refuse.
Abundance is a detail of paragraph 2, and the passage never predicts phages will replace antibiotics.
Too strong: paragraph 9 says single cases cannot judge a therapy, and 'any' infection goes far beyond the passage.
Reverses the reason: the West turned to antibiotics, and the Soviet work was ignored, not withheld.
